clips.title: Return Address Stack: predicting returns
clips.hook: Why returns have many targets and how a hardware call/return stack predicts them
clips.summary: A return has many possible targets, one per call site, so a BTB-style single target fails. Hardware mimics the software stack: push PC+4 on a call, pop on a return, which works when call and return nesting match.
clips.videoTitle: Digital Design & Computer Architecture - Lecture 17b: Branch Prediction I (Spring 2022)

quiz.question: Why is a hardware call/return stack better than a BTB for predicting return targets?
options: Returns are conditional, so the stack stores their direction
The stack is larger than a BTB so it holds more entries
Returns always jump to PC+4 so the stack is unnecessary
A return's target varies with the call site, but nested calls and returns match, so the top of the stack gives the target
quiz.explanation: One return instruction can go to many call sites, so a cached single target mispredicts. Properly nested call/return behavior makes the stack top the right target.

clips.title: Why Branch Accuracy Matters: IPC vs Misprediction
clips.hook: Compute fetch time for 500 instructions at 100%, 99%, 90% accuracy with a 20-stage, 5-wide machine
clips.summary: A misprediction wastes N×W instruction slots, where N is the resolution latency and W is the width. With N=20, W=5 and a branch every 5 instructions, IPC falls from 5 at 100% accuracy to about 4.2 at 99% and 1.67 at 90%.
clips.videoTitle: Digital Design & Computer Architecture - Lecture 17b: Branch Prediction I (Spring 2022)

quiz.question: Pipeline depth to resolve a branch is 20, width 5, one branch per 5 instructions, 90% accuracy. Roughly what is the IPC?
quiz.explanation: 500 instructions have 100 branches and 10 mispredictions, costing 200 cycles. Together with 100 useful cycles that is 300 cycles, so IPC = 500/300 ≈ 1.67.

clips.title: Profile-Guided Code Layout for PC+4 Prediction
clips.hook: How the compiler lays out basic blocks so the likely path is the not-taken fall-through
clips.summary: With always-PC+4 prediction, the compiler uses profile data to place the most probable successor block right after the branch. This works well for biased branches, but it depends on representative profiling inputs and does nothing for 50/50 branches.
clips.videoTitle: Digital Design & Computer Architecture - Lecture 17b: Branch Prediction I (Spring 2022)

quiz.question: When does profile-guided layout fail to help a not-taken (PC+4) predictor?
options: When instructions are fixed size
When branches are near 50/50 or the profile input is unrepresentative
When branches are 99/1 biased
When basic blocks are long
quiz.explanation: Layout only helps if the branch bias is strong and matches real runs. Unbiased branches have no good fall-through choice.

clips.title: BTB plus Direction Predictor in the Fetch Stage
clips.hook: What must be predicted in one fetch cycle and how a BTB and direction predictor deliver it
clips.summary: To avoid bubbles, the fetch stage must predict whether the instruction is a branch, its direction, and its target. A BTB indexed by PC stores targets from earlier executions, and a hit also shows the instruction is a branch. The direction predictor is accessed in parallel. The next PC is the BTB target if the BTB hits and the branch is predicted taken, and PC+4 otherwise.
clips.videoTitle: Digital Design & Computer Architecture - Lecture 17b: Branch Prediction I (Spring 2022)

quiz.question: In the fetch stage, when is the next PC taken from the BTB?
options: Whenever the direction predictor says not taken
Only when the BTB misses
On any BTB hit
Only when the BTB hits and the direction predictor says taken
quiz.explanation: A hit gives the target and shows the instruction is a branch. The direction predictor must still say taken. Otherwise fetch continues at PC+4.

clips.title: Principal components, loadings and their link to the SVD
clips.hook: Eigenvectors of BᵀB, scores T = BV, and why T = UΣ from the SVD of B.
clips.summary: The eigenvectors V of C = BᵀB give directions of maximal variance, and projecting the centered data gives the principal components T = BV (the loadings are V). If B = UΣVᵀ, then T = BV = UΣ, so PCA can be obtained directly from the SVD of the mean-subtracted data without forming the covariance matrix.
clips.videoTitle: Principal Component Analysis (PCA)

quiz.question: If the centered data matrix has SVD B = UΣVᵀ, what are the principal component scores T = BV?
options: T = Σ Vᵀ
T = U
T = U Σ
T = V Σ
quiz.explanation: BV = UΣVᵀV = UΣ because V has orthonormal columns. The columns of V are the eigenvectors of BᵀB (the loadings).

clips.title: Explained variance: choosing the number of components
clips.hook: Eigenvalues are squared singular values; use cumulative variance ratio to pick k.
clips.summary: The eigenvalues of the covariance matrix equal the squared singular values and give the variance along each principal component. The fraction of variance captured by the first r components is Σ_{k≤r} λ_k / Σ_all λ_k, and a common criterion is to keep enough components to reach e.g. 95%.
clips.videoTitle: Principal Component Analysis (PCA)

quiz.question: How do you decide how many principal components to keep using a 95% variance criterion?
options: Keep components whose singular values exceed 1
Keep r = n/20 components
Keep components until the mean of the data reaches zero
Choose smallest r with sum of first r eigenvalues / sum of all eigenvalues ≥ 0.95
quiz.explanation: Eigenvalues λ_k = σ_k² are the variances along each component, so the cumulative ratio measures the fraction of total variance retained.

clips.title: unique_ptr deleters: default_delete, FILE* and OpenSSL
clips.hook: The second template parameter of unique_ptr encodes what cleanup responsibility it carries.
clips.summary: unique_ptr's second template parameter defaults to default_delete, whose operator() calls delete (or delete[] for arrays). A custom deleter functor such as one calling fclose or X509_REQ_free turns C resource handles into RAII-managed owners, and the deleter type documents the responsibility.
clips.videoTitle: CppCon 2019: Arthur O'Dwyer “Back to Basics: Smart Pointers”

quiz.question: What does the deleter template parameter of unique_ptr determine?
options: Whether the unique_ptr is copyable
What operation runs on the held pointer when the unique_ptr is destroyed
The allocator used for make_unique
The thread-safety of the pointer
quiz.explanation: The destructor invokes the deleter's operator() on the pointer; default_delete calls delete, a custom one may call fclose etc.

clips.title: shared_ptr internals: the separate control block
clips.hook: Where the reference count lives, why shared_ptr is two pointers wide, and one block per object.
clips.summary: Since arbitrary types have no refcount member, shared_ptr allocates a heap control block per controlled object (not per shared_ptr) holding atomic strong and weak counts and optionally a deleter. Each shared_ptr stores a pointer to the object plus a pointer to the control block; copying increments the count and the last destruction destroys the object.
clips.videoTitle: CppCon 2019: Arthur O'Dwyer “Back to Basics: Smart Pointers”

quiz.question: How many control blocks exist for an object managed by three copies of a shared_ptr made by copying?
options: One per controlled object
Two: one strong, one weak
Zero; the count is stored in the object
Three, one per shared_ptr
quiz.explanation: The control block is per controlled object; copies share it and only increment its count.

clips.title: Why the control block stores its own pointer and deleter
clips.hook: Multiple inheritance offsets and shared_ptr to base: why ownership lives in the control block.
clips.summary: With multiple inheritance a base subobject pointer can be offset from the complete object, so shared_ptr<Vegetable> may not point at the allocation start. The control block stores the original pointer and deletion action fixed at first construction, decoupling the stored pointer from ownership; this also enables the aliasing constructor.
clips.videoTitle: CppCon 2019: Arthur O'Dwyer “Back to Basics: Smart Pointers”

quiz.question: Why does the control block keep its own pointer to the object rather than relying on the shared_ptr's pointer?
options: To support weak_ptr only
The shared_ptr's pointer may be a base-subobject pointer at an offset or point elsewhere, so deletion must use the original pointer
Because shared_ptr cannot hold a pointer
To make the count atomic
quiz.explanation: Shared_ptr<Base> or aliasing pointers may differ from the allocation address, so the control block holds the right pointer and deleter.

clips.title: make_shared: one allocation for object and control block
clips.hook: How make_shared fuses the two allocations and why it beats shared_ptr(new T).
clips.summary: shared_ptr(new T) performs two allocations, while make_shared can place the object and control block contiguously in one allocation and free them together. Factory functions also keep raw new out of application code, avoiding the double-control-block bug.
clips.videoTitle: CppCon 2019: Arthur O'Dwyer “Back to Basics: Smart Pointers”

quiz.question: What performance advantage does make_shared<T>() commonly have over shared_ptr<T>(new T)?
options: It does one allocation for object and control block instead of two
It stores the object on the stack
It avoids atomic counts
It disables the weak count
quiz.explanation: Both are placed in one contiguous block, so a single malloc/free.

clips.title: weak_ptr and the weak reference count
clips.hook: How weak_ptr keeps the control block alive after the object is destroyed and detects expiry.
clips.summary: A weak_ptr has the same layout as shared_ptr and points to the same control block, but increments the weak count. When the strong count hits zero the object is destroyed while the control block survives until weak count is zero, letting weak_ptr detect expiry.
clips.videoTitle: CppCon 2019: Arthur O'Dwyer “Back to Basics: Smart Pointers”

quiz.question: After the last shared_ptr dies but a weak_ptr remains, what is still alive?
options: The controlled object only
Nothing
The shared_ptr's stack frame
The control block, with strong count zero
quiz.explanation: The weak count keeps the control block alive so the weak_ptr can observe that the strong count is zero.

clips.title: make_shared with weak_ptr: memory held until weak refs die
clips.hook: A trade-off of make_shared's fused allocation when weak_ptrs outlive the object.
clips.summary: With make_shared the object's destructor runs when the strong count hits zero, but the single allocation can't be partially freed, so the memory is returned only after the last weak_ptr is gone. With many long-lived weak_ptrs, a custom wrapper with separate allocations may be preferable.
clips.videoTitle: CppCon 2019: Arthur O'Dwyer “Back to Basics: Smart Pointers”

quiz.question: With std::make_shared, when is the object's memory released if a weak_ptr outlives all shared_ptrs?
options: Immediately when the last shared_ptr dies
Never
When lock() is called
Only after the last weak_ptr is gone, though the destructor already ran
quiz.explanation: Object and control block share one allocation, so memory is freed with the control block, but the destructor runs earlier.

clips.title: weak_ptr as a ticket: lock() and the if-init idiom
clips.hook: Why weak_ptr can't be dereferenced and how lock() safely redeems it.
clips.summary: weak_ptr is not dereferenceable; it is a ticket to obtain a shared_ptr. lock() returns a null shared_ptr if expired, otherwise a shared_ptr that bumps the strong count, whereas the explicit shared_ptr constructor throws bad_weak_ptr.
clips.videoTitle: CppCon 2019: Arthur O'Dwyer “Back to Basics: Smart Pointers”

quiz.question: What does weak_ptr::lock() return if the object has been destroyed?
options: It blocks until recreated
A dangling shared_ptr
An empty (null) shared_ptr
It throws bad_weak_ptr
quiz.explanation: lock() returns a null shared_ptr on expiry; the explicit constructor is the one that throws.

clips.title: enable_shared_from_this: an object as its own ticket
clips.hook: How a hidden weak_ptr member lets an object get a shared_ptr to itself, and why CRTP is used.
clips.summary: enable_shared_from_this<T> holds a weak_ptr to the object's control block, set by shared_ptr's constructor when it takes ownership, and shared_from_this() locks it. It uses CRTP so the base can name the derived type in its return type.
clips.videoTitle: CppCon 2019: Arthur O'Dwyer “Back to Basics: Smart Pointers”

quiz.question: How does the weak_ptr inside enable_shared_from_this get initialized?
options: By the first call to shared_from_this()
By the Widget's constructor
By shared_ptr's constructor when it takes ownership of an object deriving from the base
By operator new
quiz.explanation: shared_ptr detects the base and sets the weak_ptr to the control block; raw new objects therefore don't work.

clips.subtopic: TCP congestion control slow start AIMD
clips.syllabus: TCP flow control (sliding window) vs congestion control (slow start, AIMD); Nagle and delayed ACK
clips.title: AIMD: Sawtooth Probing and Loss Reactions in TCP
clips.hook: Why TCP adds one MSS per RTT, halves on triple dup ACK, and resets to 1 on timeout.
clips.summary: TCP detects congestion end-to-end via loss, increasing its rate by 1 MSS per RTT and halving on a triple-duplicate-ACK loss, producing a sawtooth. A timeout is treated as more severe and resets the window to one segment.
clips.videoTitle: 3 7 TCP Congestion Control

quiz.question: In classic TCP (Reno-style) AIMD, how does the sender react to a loss detected by a timeout versus triple duplicate ACKs?
options: Timeout: cwnd halved; triple dup ACK: cwnd reset to 1 MSS
Both reset cwnd to 1 MSS
Timeout: cwnd resets to 1 MSS; triple dup ACK: cwnd is halved
Both halve cwnd
quiz.explanation: Triple duplicate ACKs indicate the network is still delivering segments, so a multiplicative decrease by half suffices; a timeout suggests severe congestion so cwnd drops to 1 MSS.

clips.subtopic: TCP congestion control slow start AIMD
clips.syllabus: TCP flow control (sliding window) vs congestion control (slow start, AIMD); Nagle and delayed ACK
clips.title: cwnd, Slow Start and the ssthresh Switch to Congestion Avoidance
clips.hook: How cwnd maps to sending rate (cwnd/RTT), why slow start is exponential, and what ssthresh does.
clips.summary: The congestion window limits unacknowledged data, giving rate ≈ cwnd/RTT. Slow start doubles cwnd every RTT from 1 MSS, and on loss ssthresh is set to half the cwnd, so slow start ends there and additive increase begins.
clips.videoTitle: 3 7 TCP Congestion Control

quiz.question: After a loss event at cwnd = 16 MSS, what is ssthresh and what happens when cwnd later reaches it?
options: ssthresh = 16 MSS; TCP stops increasing cwnd
ssthresh = 8 MSS; TCP switches from linear to exponential growth
ssthresh = 1 MSS; TCP stays in slow start
ssthresh = 8 MSS; TCP switches from exponential to linear growth
quiz.explanation: ssthresh is set to half of cwnd at loss. Slow start's exponential growth continues until cwnd reaches ssthresh, then congestion avoidance adds 1 MSS per RTT.

clips.subtopic: TCP congestion control slow start AIMD
clips.syllabus: TCP flow control (sliding window) vs congestion control (slow start, AIMD); Nagle and delayed ACK
clips.title: TCP CUBIC: Probing Around W_max with a Cubic Function
clips.hook: Why CUBIC ramps quickly toward the last loss window and then slows down near it.
clips.summary: CUBIC remembers W_max, the window at the last loss, and grows cwnd as a cubic function of the time remaining until it would reach W_max. Growth is fast far from W_max and slow near it, giving higher average throughput than linear AIMD.
clips.videoTitle: 3 7 TCP Congestion Control

quiz.question: How does CUBIC's window growth behave relative to AIMD after a loss?
options: Slower than linear far from W_max, faster near W_max
Faster than linear when far below W_max, slower as it approaches W_max
Same linear growth but with a larger multiplicative decrease
Always exponential until the next loss
quiz.explanation: Growth depends on the cube of the time difference to the target time for reaching W_max, so it is steep far from W_max and flattens near it.

clips.subtopic: TCP congestion control slow start AIMD
clips.syllabus: TCP flow control (sliding window) vs congestion control (slow start, AIMD); Nagle and delayed ACK
clips.title: Delay-Based Congestion Control: Keep the Pipe Just Full
clips.hook: Use cwnd/RTT_measured versus cwnd/RTT_min to detect queue buildup before any packet loss.
clips.summary: The sender takes RTT_min as the uncongested RTT, so the uncongested throughput is cwnd/RTT_min. If measured throughput is close to that, it increases cwnd. If it falls below that, queues are building and it decreases cwnd, avoiding loss. BBR is a deployed example.
clips.videoTitle: 3 7 TCP Congestion Control

quiz.question: In a delay-based scheme, what indicates that the bottleneck queue is building?
options: RTT_min increases
The receiver advertises a smaller window
cwnd/RTT_measured falls well below cwnd/RTT_min
A triple duplicate ACK
quiz.explanation: A higher measured RTT means queuing delay at the bottleneck, so throughput computed as cwnd/RTT_measured drops below the uncongested cwnd/RTT_min. The sender then reduces cwnd.

clips.subtopic: TCP congestion control slow start AIMD
clips.syllabus: TCP flow control (sliding window) vs congestion control (slow start, AIMD); Nagle and delayed ACK
clips.title: Why AIMD Converges to Fairness: The Two-Flow Phase Plot
clips.hook: A geometric argument showing additive increase and multiplicative decrease drive two flows to equal share.
clips.summary: Additive increase moves two flows' throughputs along a 45° line, preserving their difference. Each multiplicative decrease halves the difference, so repeated cycles converge to the equal-share line from any starting point.
clips.videoTitle: 3 7 TCP Congestion Control

quiz.question: Why does AIMD push two competing flows toward equal bandwidth shares?
options: Both flows decrease to exactly R/2 on every loss
Additive increase narrows the gap and multiplicative decrease keeps it constant
The router allocates bandwidth equally
Additive increase keeps the throughput gap constant, while each multiplicative decrease shrinks it
quiz.explanation: Equal additive increments preserve the difference between flows. Halving both rates halves the difference, so the gap shrinks geometrically over loss cycles.

clips.title: Missing join condition: Cartesian product and duplicate rows
clips.hook: What happens when the join predicate is dropped, and why joins repeat rows.
clips.summary: With no join predicate, the filters apply to enrolled only. Every surviving enrollment is then paired with every student, which is a Cartesian product. Joined rows also repeat a student's name once per matching enrollment, because SQL works on bags.
clips.videoTitle: 02 - Intermediate SQL (CMU Intro to Database Systems / Fall 2021)

quiz.question: A query lists FROM enrolled e, student s and filters only on e.grade and e.cid, with no e.sid = s.sid. What does it return?
options: Each filtered enrollment paired with every student, a Cartesian product
An error because the join is missing
Each student paired with their own enrollment only
Only the students who got the grade
quiz.explanation: Without a join predicate, each row that passes the filters is combined with every student row.

clips.title: Why non-aggregated columns break an aggregate query
clips.hook: Why selecting a course id next to AVG(gpa) is ill-defined, and how engines differ.
clips.summary: An aggregate collapses a bag of tuples into one value, so a non-aggregated column in the select list has no well-defined value. Postgres and MySQL reject the query. SQLite returns an arbitrary value from some row, because the standard does not define it.
clips.videoTitle: 02 - Intermediate SQL (CMU Intro to Database Systems / Fall 2021)

quiz.question: Why is SELECT AVG(s.gpa), e.cid FROM enrolled e JOIN student s ... (no GROUP BY) ill-formed?
options: AVG requires DISTINCT
The aggregate yields one value for the whole input, so e.cid has no single well-defined value
AVG cannot be used with joins
cid must be an integer
quiz.explanation: The aggregate collapses all rows into one output row, and many different cid values exist in that input.

clips.title: HAVING: filtering on aggregates after grouping
clips.hook: Why a WHERE predicate cannot test AVG(gpa), and what HAVING does instead.
clips.summary: WHERE is evaluated per tuple before aggregates are known. HAVING filters groups after aggregation, so it can test aggregate values. In standard SQL the aggregate expression must be repeated in HAVING rather than referenced by its select alias.
clips.videoTitle: 02 - Intermediate SQL (CMU Intro to Database Systems / Fall 2021)

quiz.question: Why can't AVG(s.gpa) > 3.9 go in the WHERE clause of a GROUP BY query?
options: AVG is not allowed with joins
WHERE runs after HAVING
WHERE only accepts constants
WHERE is evaluated per tuple before the group aggregates are computed
quiz.explanation: The group average is only known after all tuples are aggregated. HAVING is applied to the groups after that.

clips.title: Nested subqueries: IN, ANY, ALL and scoping
clips.hook: How an inner query feeds an outer query, and how subquery operators differ.
clips.summary: A subquery acts like a function returning a result set to the outer query. The scope of a column name such as sid depends on which query block it appears in. The quantifiers ALL, ANY, IN and EXISTS test the outer value against the subquery rows. A join can express the same query, and subqueries are often hard for optimizers to rewrite.
clips.videoTitle: 02 - Intermediate SQL (CMU Intro to Database Systems / Fall 2021)

quiz.question: What does `x = ANY (subquery)` require?
options: x is greater than all rows
x equals every row of the subquery
x equals at least one row of the subquery
The subquery returns no rows
quiz.explanation: ANY is satisfied if the comparison holds for at least one subquery row, which is why IN is equivalent to = ANY.

clips.syllabus: Cache memory: hierarchy, locality, mapping (direct / set-associative / fully associative)
clips.title: N-way set-associative cache as N parallel DM caches
clips.hook: Sets, ways, index bits and why only N comparators are needed however large the cache.
clips.summary: An N-way SA cache is N direct-mapped sub-caches (ways) in parallel; the index selects a set of N lines, any of which may hold the block. It tolerates up to N conflicting blocks per index while needing only N comparators, and the number of ways need not be a power of two since no address bits select a way.
clips.videoTitle: 14.2.9 Associative Caches

quiz.question: A 4-way SA cache has 8 lines per way. How many sets and how many tag comparators does it have?
options: 32 sets, 4 comparators
8 sets, 32 comparators
8 sets, 4 comparators
4 sets, 8 comparators
quiz.explanation: Each index selects one line from each of 4 ways, giving 8 sets of 4 lines, and 4 comparators are used in parallel.

clips.title: How many ways? Associativity vs. hit time and AMAT
clips.hook: Why returns diminish beyond 4-8 ways and how extra ways hurt hit time.
clips.summary: Only a few conflicting regions (code, stack, data) are active at a time, so a small number of ways avoids most conflicts. Beyond about 4-8 ways, miss ratio barely improves while combining hit signals adds delay to hit time and AMAT, so 8-way performs close to FA.
clips.videoTitle: 14.2.9 Associative Caches

quiz.question: Why does increasing associativity beyond about 8 ways often fail to improve AMAT?
options: Blocks can no longer be evicted
Tags become longer than the index
Compulsory misses increase
Miss ratio gains are tiny while hit-signal combining logic increases hit time
quiz.explanation: AMAT = hit time + miss ratio x penalty; extra ways add hit-time delay with negligible miss-ratio reduction.

clips.syllabus: Cache write policies (write-through/back), replacement, miss types (3 Cs)
clips.title: Replacement policies: LRU cost, FIFO, random
clips.hook: Why LRU needs log2(8!) = 16 bits per 8-way set and why real caches approximate it.
clips.summary: Optimal replacement evicts the block used furthest in the future, which is unknowable, so LRU predicts using locality. True LRU for an 8-way set needs log2(8!) = 16 state bits and costly update logic, so hardware uses approximations, FIFO or random; all but random can be adversarially defeated.
clips.videoTitle: 14.2.9 Associative Caches

quiz.question: How many bits are needed to encode the exact LRU ordering of one 8-way set?
quiz.explanation: There are 8! = 40320 orderings, and ceil(log2(40320)) = 16 bits.

clips.title: Log-uniform random search and default learning rates
clips.hook: Why a shared search range can silently bias an optimizer comparison, even with random search.
clips.summary: Random search over learning rate samples the exponent uniformly (log-uniform, e.g. 1e-4 to 1). If a shared range is centered on one optimizer's default (SGD momentum 1e-2) but not another's (Adam 1e-3), the comparison is biased toward the former.
clips.videoTitle: Descending through a Crowded Valley -- Benchmarking Deep Learning Optimizers (Paper Explained)

quiz.question: A benchmark samples learning rates log-uniformly from [1e-4, 1] for every optimizer. Why does this favor momentum SGD (default 1e-2) over Adam (default 1e-3)?
options: Log-uniform sampling only works for SGD
1e-2 sits at the center of the log range while 1e-3 is off-center, so random search covers the region near SGD's good value more densely
Log-uniform sampling samples the learning rate itself uniformly, favoring large values
Adam cannot use learning rates below 1e-2
quiz.explanation: Log-uniform sampling draws the exponent uniformly, so 1e-2 is the midpoint of [1e-4, 1]. Adam's typical optimum (about 1e-3) lies off-center, so fewer samples land near it.

clips.title: Tuning on a single seed: why hyperparameter selection can mislead
clips.hook: Tune on one seed, test on ten: how a lucky or unlucky tuning seed biases the chosen learning rate.
clips.summary: Tuning a learning rate on a single seed can select a value that suits that particular initialization, for example a small step size that works near a cliff in the loss landscape. The value may then perform badly from other initializations, so averaging only the test runs does not remove the tuning bias.
clips.videoTitle: Descending through a Crowded Valley -- Benchmarking Deep Learning Optimizers (Paper Explained)

quiz.question: Hyperparameters are tuned on one random seed, then the best setting is evaluated over 10 other seeds. What is the main risk?
options: Different seeds change the model architecture
The chosen setting may overfit the tuning seed's initialization, so test results reflect tuning luck rather than the optimizer's average quality
The validation loss becomes undefined
The test average has higher variance than tuning
quiz.explanation: Selection happens on a single noisy sample of initialization, so the chosen learning rate can be specific to that start point. Averaging the test runs doesn't remove that selection bias.

clips.syllabus: Gradients, convexity, gradient descent, learning rate; SGD vs momentum vs Adam
clips.title: Is tuning Adam the same as switching optimizers?
clips.hook: Why trying different optimizers with defaults helps about as much as tuning one: effective learning rate.
clips.summary: The paper finds that tuning one optimizer's hyperparameters gains about as much as trying several optimizers at their defaults. A plausible explanation is that each optimizer's learning rate enters its update rule differently, so switching optimizers changes the effective learning rate, which is itself a form of tuning.
clips.videoTitle: Descending through a Crowded Valley -- Benchmarking Deep Learning Optimizers (Paper Explained)

quiz.question: Why might switching between SGD with momentum, Adam and RMSProp at default settings help as much as tuning one optimizer's learning rate?
options: Each optimizer's default learning rate enters its update differently, so switching changes the effective step size, a hidden form of learning-rate tuning
Adam has no learning rate
Default parameters are always optimal
All of them are exactly equivalent algorithms
quiz.explanation: The same numeric learning rate yields different effective step sizes in different update rules. Choosing a different optimizer therefore partly amounts to choosing a different effective learning rate.
